extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Literature-review style guidance on how outside actors (advertisers, public relations, and government) influence news coverage and what indicators, practices, and ethical standards identify or mitigate that influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser influence over content
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers have 'substantial influence over what is and is not emphasized in the media,' which may be subtle and indirect or, increasingly, direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include advertisers requiring advance summaries of major themes/articles, asking to be informed if content covers sexual/political/social/controversial topics, requesting rescheduling of ads when unfavorable stories appear, pulling ads in response to coverage, and applying economic pressure to influence story selection or kill stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants of whose influence prevails (Baker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence or favor tends to go toward (1) the larger purchaser; (2) the purchaser with the most knowledge as to how the media can serve its needs; and (3) the purchaser most sensitive to how the media can affect its interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing advertiser effects, consider advertiser size, media-savviness, and sensitivity to media impacts as predictors of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple loyalties of managers
rubrics_metrics.description: Media managers face multiple loyalties—viewers, stockholders, and advertisers—which shape editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editorial outcomes in light of these competing pressures; policy or ethical guidelines should account for these multiple accountability lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical indicators of advertiser pressure (survey metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys of editors and journalists provide quantitative indicators of advertiser pressure: e.g., ~90% reported advertisers tried to influence story types and used economic pressure; ~70% said advertisers tried to kill stories; ~37% reported bowing to advertiser pressures while 85% still carried critical stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reported frequencies (percentages) from surveys as evidence of the prevalence and severity of advertiser pressure in newsrooms; track changes over time and by medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of newsroom ethical discussions on advertiser pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical discussions about advertiser pressures (e.g., 'blurbs,' 'business-office musts') are infrequent in many newsrooms—reported by some editors as occurring 'less than once a year or never.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, documented ethical discussion is a protective practice; absence of such discussions is an indicator of vulnerability to commercial influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium and outlet susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast (radio and television) is more susceptible to advertiser pressures than print because of greater sensitivity to profit needs and reliance on advertising revenue; local television is especially vulnerable compared to national outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess vulnerability by medium and outlet size: local and small stations tend to show higher rates of pressure/compromise than national outlets or print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on information subsidies (public relations materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners provide 'information subsidies' (press releases, PSAs, VNRs, press conferences) at no cost; news organizations, facing budget and staffing pressures, often use these subsidies to fill news holes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating news content should account for the proportion and role of information subsidies; reliance increases when newsrooms are under-resourced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance and use rates of PR materials as influence metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies report high usage rates of PR materials in news: examples include >50% of environmental stories from releases in one study, 51% of government public info officer subsidies used by newspapers, assignment editors reporting 90% use of releases to develop stories, and varying TV acceptance rates (e.g., 59% acceptance at small TV stations in one study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure PR influence by acceptance/usage rates, types of sources retained (government, nonprofit, business), and whether materials are run 'as is' or incorporated with independent reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of journalist–public relations practitioner relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: The relationship between journalists and PR practitioners affects usage: some survey/interview evidence shows improving relations (45% positive/very positive), but a persistent minority view it as 'love/hate' or a 'necessary evil.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how practitioners and journalists perceive each other; more positive, collaborative relationships may increase use of subsidies but also enable checks and balances if trust includes transparency expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and disclosure for non-editorial video and audio (RTNDA guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: RTNDA guideline: 'News managers and producers should clearly disclose the origin of information and label all material provided by corporate or other non-editorial sources.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure examples: show the organization's logo, or have an anchor say 'This video was provided by...'. Executives should ask whether more than one side is included, whether there is a financial agenda, whether viewers would believe it's produced locally, and whether editorial staff could have produced the material themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid airing VNRs 'as is' or disguising sponsored content
rubrics_metrics.description: Stations have been found to run VNRs 'as is' and actively disguise sponsored content to make it appear to be their own reporting; this practice conflicts with ethical guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: do not present externally produced material as station reporting; balance client-supplied material with independent footage and basic journalistic research; explicitly label sponsored content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewers' right to know news origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle: 'viewers have a right to know where their news comes from.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency about source origins preserves audience trust; nondisclosure removes an audience's ability to scrutinize potential bias or agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use of prepackaged news and constraints on government PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Government agencies distribute prepackaged news (VNRs, releases) and use information specialists to 'ensure that the nation's public media carry the desired message forward'; legal constraints include the Gillett Amendment/1972 public law limiting use of appropriated funds for publicity or propaganda to influence legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating content, identify government-originated materials and assess timing, scripting, and alignment with policy/administration agendas; ensure legal/ethical constraints and disclosure are observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing, agenda-building, and indexing to official sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials and PR actors use routine news channels (press conferences, official proceedings, press releases) to set frames and agendas; journalists often 'index' slant to governmental elites' opinions, making framing an effective strategic tool for actors seeking favorable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news for framing effects and the dominance of official sources; consider whether coverage echoes elite perspectives disproportionately and whether alternative frames or sources are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct political pressure and censorship appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Political actors can exert direct pressure on publishers and news organizations (e.g., Kennedy's encouragement that publishers censor content), not just indirect agenda-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor for direct appeals, warnings, or interventions by government or political actors and treat such incidents as explicit threats to editorial independence requiring institutional safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether content includes multiple sides and independent verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives should determine 'whether more than one side is included, if there is a financial agenda to releasing the story, and if the viewers…would believe this is work done locally by [their] team.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a checklist before airing externally produced material: check for balance, financial interest disclosure, and the feasibility of independent editorial production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/resource constraints as predictors of PR/VNR use
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller newsrooms and outlets facing budget cuts are more likely to accept and use information subsidies; resource limitations correlate with higher acceptance rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring susceptibility, account for newsroom staffing and budget as explanatory variables for reliance on PR materials.
